Ch 1: Fluid Properties & Pressure

Lecture 1.1 · Text Ch 1.1–1.7 · Week of May 4th

1.1 — Introduction

Fluid mechanics studies how fluids (liquids and gases) behave at rest and in motion. It is one of the most broadly applicable areas in engineering — spanning aerodynamics, marine propulsion, biomedical devices, renewable energy, sports engineering, and environmental science. In this course, we develop governing equations using the control volume approach and apply them to practical engineering problems.

Applications of Fluid Mechanics

The reach of fluid mechanics is enormous. Some representative domains:

Transportation — helicopter vortex ring states, ship propeller vortices, CFD streamline simulations for race car aerodynamics. Understanding lift, drag, and flow separation is central to vehicle design across aviation, marine, and automotive engineering.

Biomedical — computational fluid dynamics for artificial heart pump design (modeling blood flow through impellers), lung airflow simulation through branching airways, arterial blood flow modeling for detecting aneurysms and stenosis.

Energy — water flow simulation in hydroelectric dams (velocity magnitude fields through spillways), airflow through wind turbine blades (vortex shedding and wake interactions), combustion chamber flows in gas turbines.

Environment & Geophysics — ocean current modeling for climate prediction, atmospheric pollution dispersion driven by wind patterns.

Sports — aerodynamic drag optimization of golf club heads, bobsled body shaping, cyclist helmet streamlining — all use CFD velocity field analysis to minimize drag coefficients.

The Concept of a Fluid: Classification of Matter

Matter exists in four states — solid, liquid, gas, and plasma. In this course, we focus on liquids and gases, which are collectively called fluids. The critical distinction between solids and fluids comes down to how they respond to shear stress.

Classification of matter by state. Liquids and gases are collectively called fluids.
Solid

Molecules are packed in a lattice or geometric structure with constant molecular spacing. Large cohesive forces hold molecules together, preventing relative movement except for slight vibration. When subjected to a load, a solid deforms but continues to support the load — internal shear stresses build up and reach equilibrium. A solid can resist shear stress by deforming.

Liquid

Molecules are not bound in a lattice — they are more mobile than in solids, but molecular spacing is still approximately constant. Liquids do not hold their shape; they flow and take the shape of their container, forming a horizontal free surface at the top. When confined, their intermolecular forces allow them to resist compressive forces, so liquids have constant volume and density. However, they cannot resist shear loading — instead of reaching equilibrium, they deform continuously and form waves (think of coffee sloshing in a mug).

Gas

Intermolecular forces are weak enough to allow molecules to travel freely until repelled by other molecules. Gases have no definite volume — they must be held in a container, otherwise they flow out to form an atmosphere. A gas completely fills any space it occupies. Gravitational effects are negligible compared to buoyancy forces. Gases are still classified as fluids because they flow when subjected to a force (e.g., gas flow in pipes).

A fourth state, plasma (ionized matter), exists and is critical for fusion energy research (e.g., tokamak reactors), but it is not covered in MAAE 2300.

Common examples to keep in mind: Solids — steel, aluminum, wood. Liquids — water, alcohol, oil. Gases — oxygen, nitrogen, air.

★ Key Distinction: Solid vs Fluid

A solid resists shear stress by deforming to a static equilibrium — loading causes internal shear stresses that balance the applied force. A fluid cannot resist any shear stress — it deforms continuously under even the smallest applied shear, no matter how small. This continuous deformation under shear is the defining property of a fluid. Note: this does not mean fluids have no viscosity — viscous effects resist the rate of deformation, but the fluid never reaches static equilibrium under shear.

The Concept of Continuum

At the molecular level, matter is discrete — individual molecules bouncing around with gaps between them. But in engineering, we want to treat fluid properties like density as smooth, continuous functions so we can use calculus. The continuum assumption makes this possible.

Consider measuring density by counting mass in a sample volume of size \(\delta V\):

Case 1: Volume comparable to intermolecular spacing (very small \(\delta V\)). The number of molecules inside fluctuates wildly as they move in and out. The measured density \( ho = \delta m / \delta V\) is noisy and unstable — this is microscopic uncertainty.

Case 2: Volume much larger than intermolecular spacing. The number of molecules entering roughly equals the number leaving at any instant. The measured density stabilizes to a constant value — fluctuations average out. This is the continuum regime.

Case 3: Volume too large (macroscopic scale). The density starts reflecting spatial variations across the fluid (e.g., a container with sloshing, spilling fluid) rather than a local point value — this is macroscopic uncertainty.

Density (Continuum Definition)

\[ ho = \lim_{\delta V o \delta V^*} rac{\delta m}{\delta V} \]

\( ho\) — density (kg/m³) \(\delta m\) — mass in volume element (kg) \(\delta V\) — volume element (m³) \(\delta V^*\) — smallest volume for stable density (~\(10^{-9}\) mm³)

When to use: Any problem requiring fluid density as a point property — underlies every governing equation in this course (continuity, momentum, energy).

When NOT to use: Rarefied gas flows (high altitude, vacuum systems) where the mean free path approaches the characteristic length of the problem. In those cases, molecular dynamics or kinetic theory is needed instead.

Density measured as a function of sample volume δV. Below δV*, molecular fluctuations dominate. Above δV*, density stabilizes — this is the continuum regime. At very large volumes, spatial non-uniformity introduces macroscopic uncertainty.

At standard atmospheric conditions, \(\delta V^*_{ ext{air}}\) contains approximately \(3 imes 10^7\) molecules — a sufficiently large number for a stable statistical average. Since \(\delta V^*\) is extremely small compared to any engineering dimension, density (and all other fluid properties) can be treated as smoothly varying functions of position.

★ Why Continuum Matters

The continuum assumption is what lets us write partial derivatives, integrals, and governing PDEs for fluid flow. Every equation in Ch 3–6 (continuity, momentum, energy, Bernoulli) relies on density, velocity, and pressure being differentiable functions of space and time. Without continuum, we would need molecular dynamics — computationally impractical for engineering-scale problems.

Branches of Fluid Mechanics

The field is divided into three branches, each of which we study in this course:

The three branches of fluid mechanics and their corresponding chapters in this course.
Hydrostatics

The study of fluids at rest or moving with constant velocity (no acceleration). Covers pressure distribution, forces on submerged surfaces, and buoyancy. Focus of Ch 1–2.

Kinematics

The study of the geometry of fluid motion — velocity fields, streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines — without considering the forces that cause the motion. Covered beginning in Ch 4.

Fluid Dynamics

The study of the forces that cause accelerated motion in fluids. This is where we develop and apply the momentum and energy equations using the Reynolds Transport Theorem (Ch 5–6).

1.2 — Units, Dimensional Analysis & Fluid Properties

Dimensions and Units

To describe the physical state of a fluid quantitatively, we need two concepts: dimensions (the measure by which a physical variable is expressed) and units (a particular way of attaching a number to that dimension). We use curly braces { } to denote dimensions and square brackets [ ] to denote units.

Dimension

The measure by which a physical variable is expressed quantitatively. For example, the dimension of the height of a fluid container is Length {L}.

Unit

A particular way of attaching a number to a quantitative dimension. For example, the unit of the dimension of length in the metric system is the meter [m].

Primary Dimensions

In fluid mechanics, four primary (independent) dimensions form the foundation from which all other quantities are derived:

DimensionSymbol
Mass{M}
Length{L}
Time{T}
Temperature{Θ}

A fifth primary dimension, Electric Current {I}, exists for electrically conducting fluids like liquid metals and electrolytes, but it is not used in this course. All other physical properties are derived from these four primaries. For example, force comes from Newton’s second law:

Dimension of Force

\[ \mathbf{F} = m

1.4 — Pressure

Absolute, gage & vacuum pressures • Hydrostatic distribution in oceans & atmosphere • Stacked-fluid layers • Multi-fluid manometers

Absolute, Gage & Vacuum Pressure

Recall from Section 1.3 that pressure at any point in a static fluid is a scalar — equal in all directions. Here we formalize the three reference frames engineers use to report pressure values.

Absolute Pressure

The actual pressure at a given position, measured relative to absolute vacuum (i.e., absolute zero pressure). It is always positive.

Gage Pressure

The difference between the absolute pressure and the local atmospheric pressure. Most pressure-measuring devices read zero when open to the atmosphere, so they indicate gage pressure. Gage pressure can be positive or negative.

Vacuum Pressure

When the absolute pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, we express the shortfall as vacuum pressure: \(p_{ ext{vac}} = p_{ ext{atm}} - p_{ ext{abs}}\). It is always a positive number indicating how far below atmospheric the point is.

Pressure Reference Conversions
\[ p_{ ext{abs}} = p_{ ext{gage}} + p_{ ext{atm}} \] \[ p_{ ext{abs}} = p_{ ext{atm}} - p_{ ext{vac}} \]
\(p_{ ext{abs}}\) — absolute pressure [Pa] \(p_{ ext{gage}}\) — gage pressure [Pa] \(p_{ ext{atm}}\) — local atmospheric pressure [Pa] \(p_{ ext{vac}}\) — vacuum pressure (always ≥ 0) [Pa]
Figure 1.4.1 — Relationship between absolute, gage, and vacuum pressures. Absolute vacuum is the datum (\(p_{ ext{abs}}=0\)). Gage pressure is measured from \(p_{ ext{atm}}\).
★ Key Insight

Standard atmospheric pressure is \(p_{ ext{atm}} = 101{,}325\) Pa \(= 101.325\) kPa \(= 14.696\) psi \(= 2116\) lbf/ft². When a problem says "gage pressure," it means \(p_{ ext{atm}}\) has already been subtracted. When working hydrostatic problems with a free surface open to the atmosphere, setting \(p_a = 0\) (gage) often simplifies the algebra — just be consistent.

Hydrostatic Pressure in Oceans & Atmospheres

From Section 1.3 we derived the general incompressible hydrostatic equation \(P_2 - P_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1)\). Here we apply it systematically to two common scenarios: submerging below a free surface (water) and rising above it (air).

Pressure at Depth (Below Free Surface)
\[ P = P_a + \gamma_{ ext{water}}\, h \]
\(P_a\) — atmospheric pressure at free surface [Pa] \(\gamma_{ ext{water}}\) — specific weight of the liquid [N/m³] \(h\) — depth below the free surface (positive downward) [m]

Derivation: Set \(z=0\) at the free surface with \(z\) positive upward. A point at depth \(h\) has \(z_2 = -h\). Substituting: \(P - P_a = -\gamma_{ ext{water}}(-h - 0) = +\gamma_{ ext{water}}\, h\). Pressure increases with depth.

Pressure at Altitude (Above Free Surface)
\[ P = P_a - \gamma_{ ext{air}}\, b \]
\(P_a\) — atmospheric pressure at ground level [Pa] \(\gamma_{ ext{air}}\) — specific weight of air [N/m³] \(b\) — height above the reference surface (positive upward) [m]

Derivation: At height \(z_2 = +b\) above the free surface: \(P - P_a = -\gamma_{ ext{air}}(b - 0) = -\gamma_{ ext{air}}\, b\). Pressure decreases with altitude.

★ Sign Convention Shortcut

Moving down in a fluid: add \(\gamma h\). Moving up: subtract \(\gamma h\). This rule works for every hydrostatic and manometry problem — it is equivalent to the general equation \(P_2 - P_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1)\).

Equal Pressure on Horizontal Planes

Recall from Section 1.3 that pressure depends only on vertical position in a static fluid. Here we restate this as a practical rule with an important caveat.

Same-Fluid Horizontal-Plane Rule

The pressure is the same at all points on a horizontal plane in a given fluid, regardless of container geometry, provided that the points are interconnected by a continuous path of the same fluid.

If a different fluid (e.g., mercury vs water) separates two points at the same depth, their pressures are not necessarily equal — they lack a continuous same-fluid connection.

Stacked-Fluid Layers

When a container holds multiple immiscible fluids stacked vertically, the pressure increases through each layer by \( ho_i g h_i\). This extends the basic hydrostatic equation to multi-layer systems.

Figure 1.4.2 — Left: single fluid with pressure \(P_{ ext{below}} = P_{ ext{atm}} + ho g h\). Right: three stacked fluid layers, each contributing \( ho_i g h_i\) to the total pressure at point 1.
Pressure Below Stacked Fluid Layers
\[ P_1 = P_{ ext{atm}} + ho_1 g h_1 + ho_2 g h_2 + ho_3 g h_3 \]
\(P_1\) — pressure at the bottom of the stack [Pa] \(P_{ ext{atm}}\) — atmospheric pressure at the top free surface [Pa] \( ho_i\) — density of the \(i\)-th fluid layer [kg/m³] \(h_i\) — thickness of the \(i\)-th layer [m]
★ Tip

In general, for \(N\) stacked layers: \(P = P_{ ext{atm}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} ho_i g h_i\). Each layer is treated as an incompressible fluid of constant density. The ordering of layers (which fluid is on top) matters — denser fluids sink to the bottom, so typically \( ho_1 < ho_2 < ho_3\).

Multiple-Fluid Manometer

A multiple-fluid manometer connects two pressure chambers through a series of U-tubes containing different fluids. The technique from Section 1.3 — "down adds \(\gamma h\), up subtracts \(\gamma h\), jump across at equal levels" — generalizes to any number of fluids.

Figure 1.4.3 — Multiple-fluid manometer with four fluid segments. Starting at A, trace through each leg: jump across at equal-pressure interfaces, apply \(-\gamma(z_2-z_1)\) through each fluid column.
Multi-Fluid Manometer Derivation

Starting at chamber A and walking through the manometer to chamber B:

\[ p_A - p_B = (p_A - p_1) + (p_1 - p_2) + (p_2 - p_3) + (p_3 - p_B) \]

Each pressure difference is evaluated using \(p_2 - p_1 = -\gamma(z_2 - z_1)\) with the specific weight of the fluid in that leg:

\[ p_A - p_B = -\gamma_1(z_A - z_1) - \gamma_2(z_1 - z_2) - \gamma_3(z_2 - z_3) - \gamma_4(z_3 - z_B) \]

The intermediate pressures \(p_1, p_2, p_3\) cancel because at each "jump across," we move to a point at the same elevation in the same continuous fluid — where the pressures are equal.

★ Exam Strategy

For any manometer problem: (1) pick a start point (usually the unknown), (2) trace through every fluid column — add \(\gamma h\) going down, subtract \(\gamma h\) going up, (3) jump across U-tube interfaces at the same level, (4) arrive at the other known pressure. Solve for the unknown. Never skip a fluid column.

2.1 — Hydrostatic Forces on Plane Surfaces

Resultant force on submerged surfaces • Center of pressure • Worked examples: gates, hinges & stops

Why Hydrostatic Forces?

In Chapter 1 we learned that pressure increases linearly with depth in a static incompressible fluid. That pressure acts on every submerged surface — dam faces, lock gates, tank walls, submarine hulls. To design these structures, we need to answer two questions:

(1) What is the total hydrostatic force (the "resultant force") on the surface?
(2) Where does that resultant force act (the "center of pressure")?

Knowing both the magnitude and the location of the resultant force lets us perform static equilibrium analysis on structures — finding hinge reactions, bolt forces, required counterweights, and so on.

Force on a Horizontal Surface

For a flat, horizontal surface at depth \(H\) below the free surface, the pressure is uniform across the entire area because every point is at the same depth. The resultant force is simply pressure times area:

Resultant Force — Horizontal Surface
\[ F_b = p_b \, A_b = \gamma H \, A_b \]
\(F_b\) — resultant hydrostatic force on the bottom surface [N] \(p_b = \gamma H\) — uniform gage pressure at depth \(H\) [Pa] \(A_b\) — area of the horizontal surface [m²] \(\gamma = ho g\) — specific weight of the fluid [N/m³]

Because the pressure is uniform, the resultant passes through the centroid of the surface — the center of pressure coincides with the centroid. But what about inclined or vertical surfaces where pressure varies with depth?

Force on an Inclined Plane Surface

When a plane surface is tilted at angle \( heta\) to the horizontal, the pressure on it varies linearly from top to bottom (since depth increases along the surface). The hydrostatic pressure acts perpendicular to the surface at every point, and its magnitude increases with depth.

Figure 2.1.1 — Inclined plane surface at angle \( heta\). Side view shows the free surface, depth \(h(x,y)\), centroid depth \(h_{ ext{CG}}\), and the resultant force \(F = p_{ ext{CG}} A\). Plan view shows the centroid (CG) and center of pressure (CP) on the surface.

We define a coordinate \(\xi\) measured along the inclined surface from the free-surface intersection line. The depth at any point relates to \(\xi\) by \(h = \xi \sin heta\). A local coordinate system \((x, y)\) is centered at the centroid (CG) of the surface, with \(y\) pointing up-slope (toward the free surface).

Resultant Force

Derivation of Resultant Force

The total force on the inclined surface is the integral of pressure over area:

\[ F = \int p \, dA = \int (p_a + \gamma h) \, dA = p_a A + \gamma \int h \, dA \]

Substituting \(h = \xi \sin heta\):

\[ F = p_a A + \gamma \sin heta \int \xi \, dA \]

The integral \(\int \xi \, dA\) is recognized as \(\xi_{ ext{CG}}

Ch 4: Introduction to Fluid Dynamics

Lecture 4.1 · Text Ch 1.5, 3.1, 6.1–6.2, 1.9, 3.2 · Week of May 25th

4.1 — Introduction to Fluid Dynamics

Everything so far has dealt with fluids at rest — pressure distributions, hydrostatic forces, buoyancy. Now the fluid starts to move, and the central question changes from “what force does the fluid exert?” to “how do we describe the motion?” This lecture builds the vocabulary and the bookkeeping tools for the rest of the course: how to describe a flow field, how to picture it, how to classify it, and how to measure how much fluid is passing through a section.

Key Definitions

Fluid Statics

The study of fluids at rest. There is no relative motion between fluid particles, so no shear stresses act — pressure is the only stress. (This was Chapters 1–3.)

Kinematics

The study of the geometry of motion, without reference to the forces that cause it. The fundamental kinematic quantities describe four things a fluid element can do: translation, rotation, linear deformation (stretching), and angular deformation (shearing).

Fluid Dynamics

The study of fluids in motion, including the forces and energy involved. This is where the course is headed — continuity, momentum, and energy equations.

Fluid Kinematics

The study of the geometry of fluid motion — how fluids flow and how to describe that flow mathematically, before bringing forces into the picture.

Two Ways to Describe Fluid Motion

A flow contains an enormous number of fluid particles. There are two fundamentally different bookkeeping strategies for describing what they are doing.

Lagrangian Description

Pick a fluid particle and follow it. Keep track of the position and velocity of each individual particle as it moves — and do this simultaneously for every particle in the flow field. This is intuitive (it is just Newtonian particle mechanics applied to fluid blobs), but tracking billions of particles at once is hopeless for most engineering problems.

Eulerian Description

Forget individual particles. Instead, fix your attention on points in space (a region called the flow domain or control volume) and record what the fluid is doing as it passes through each point. Rather than following particles, we define field variables — functions of space and time — such as the pressure field \(p(x,y,z,t)\) and the velocity field \( ec{V}(x,y,z,t)\), defined at every location and instant.

Two descriptions of the same flow. Lagrangian follows individual particles; Eulerian fixes points in space and records the field variables of whatever fluid is there.
The Velocity Field (Eulerian)

In Cartesian coordinates the velocity field has three scalar components, each a function of position and time:

\[ ec{V} = (u,\,v,\,w) = u(x,y,z,t)\, ec{i} + v(x,y,z,t)\, ec{j} + w(x,y,z,t)\, ec{k} \]

\( ec{V}\) — velocity vector at a point (m/s) \(u,\,v,\,w\) — x, y, z velocity components (m/s) \( ec{i},\, ec{j},\, ec{k}\) — unit vectors along x, y, z \(x,y,z\) — position; \(t\) — time

When to use: Any time you need the velocity at a location (not on a specific particle) — finding stagnation points, plugging into continuity/momentum/energy, evaluating flow rate across a section.

When NOT to use: If you genuinely need the history of one particle (e.g. a tracer's path), that is a Lagrangian question — integrate \(d ec{x}/dt = ec{V}\) along the particle instead.

★ Key Convention for This Course

We use the Eulerian description throughout MAAE 2300. It does not distinguish individual particles — we look only at the total effect within a control volume. This is what makes the control-volume governing equations (continuity, momentum, energy) possible.

Worked Example — Finding a Stagnation Point

Problem: A steady, incompressible, two-dimensional velocity field is given by

\[ ec{V} = (u,v) = (0.5 + 0.8x)\, ec{i} + (1.5 - 0.8y)\, ec{j} \]

where x and y are in metres and velocity is in m/s. A stagnation point is a location where the velocity is zero. Determine whether any stagnation points exist and, if so, where.

Solution

Thought process: A vector is zero only if every component is zero. So set each scalar component to zero and solve the two equations independently — one gives x, the other gives y.

Assumptions: Flow is steady (no time dependence) and two-dimensional (no z-component, no variation with z), exactly as stated.

Step 1 — Set the x-component to zero:

\[ u = 0.5 + 0.8x = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x = - rac{0.5}{0.8} = -0.625\ ext{m} \]

Step 2 — Set the y-component to zero:

\[ v = 1.5 - 0.8y = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; y = rac{1.5}{0.8} = 1.875\ ext{m} \]

Step 3 — Combine. Both conditions are satisfied at exactly one point:

\[ oxed{ ext{One stagnation point at } (x,y) = (-0.625\ ext{m},\ 1.875\ ext{m})} \]

★ Tip: Because each component depends on only one coordinate here, the solution is unique. If a component were a function of both x and y, you would solve the two equations simultaneously and could get several stagnation points (or none).

Flow Visualization: Lines of Flow

Fluid mechanics is a highly visual subject. We use sketches and photographs to extract qualitative and quantitative information about a flow. There are four standard families of lines used to picture a flow: streamlines, pathlines, streaklines, and timelines. They are defined differently, and — importantly — they only coincide under special conditions.

Streamline

A line that is everywhere tangent to the velocity at a given instant. Key properties:

• The fluid velocity is tangent to the streamline at every point on it.
• Streamlines do not cross — if they did, the velocity at the crossing point would have two directions, which is impossible. There is a unique velocity at each point in space.
• Streamlines can change with time in an unsteady flow (they are an instantaneous snapshot).

Streamlines (teal) with the velocity vector (orange) tangent at each point. The arrows show flow direction; streamlines never intersect.
Streamtube

A bundle of streamlines that surrounds a region of flow. Because the bounding lines are streamlines, the velocity is tangent to the walls — so no fluid crosses the walls of a streamtube; flow is contained inside it like fluid in a conduit. In 2-D, a streamtube is formed by just two streamlines.

A streamtube: the two outer streamlines (navy) act like solid walls because no flow crosses them. Interior streamlines carry the flow through.
Pathline

The actual path traced by a single particle as it travels over a period of time \(0 \le t \le t_n\). It can be obtained experimentally: release one particle into the flow and take a long-exposure photograph. A pathline is a time history of one particle.

A pathline: one particle photographed at successive instants. The dashed curve is the route a single particle actually followed.
Streakline

The line connecting all particles that have passed through one fixed point, photographed at a single instant \(t = t_n\). Every particle on a streakline shares the same origin. Physically, a streakline is what you see when you continuously inject dye or smoke from a point in the flow — the visible streak of dye is the streakline.

A streakline: the locus, at one instant, of every particle that has passed through the injection point. This is the dye/smoke streak you see in a wind tunnel.
Timeline

A set of fluid particles that form a line at a given instant. Mark a row of adjacent particles at one moment, then watch how that row distorts as the flow carries it along — the deformation of a timeline reveals velocity gradients (shear) in the flow.

A timeline: a straight row of particles marked at \(t_0\) distorts into a curve at \(t_1\). The bending shows the velocity varies across the row (shear).
★ Key Result: Steady Flow

In general these four line families are different. But in steady flow, streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines all coincide. If the velocity field never changes in time, then the instantaneous tangent direction (streamline), the path one particle follows (pathline), and the dye streak (streakline) are the same curve. This is why dye and smoke can be used to reveal “the streamlines” of a steady flow — tools like Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and CFD do this quantitatively.

In steady flow the three curves lie on top of one another (drawn slightly offset here only so all three are visible). They are physically the same line.

Classifying Flows: Steady, Unsteady, Uniform

Two independent yes/no questions classify a flow. Does it change with time? (steady vs unsteady) and does it change with location? (uniform vs non-uniform). These are separate ideas — do not conflate them.

Steady Flow

The velocity at a given point in space does not vary with time: \(\partial ec{V}/\partial t = 0\) at every fixed point. The flow pattern is frozen even though individual particles keep moving through it.

Unsteady Flow

The velocity at a point changes with time. Unsteady flows may be nonperiodic (e.g. a valve being opened), periodic (e.g. pulsating pump flow), or truly random (turbulence).

Uniform Flow

The velocity at a given instant does not vary with location over the region of interest. (This is about spatial variation, not time — a flow can be steady but non-uniform, like flow speeding up through a nozzle.)

★ Don't Confuse These

Steady/unsteady is about time (\(\partial/\partial t\)); uniform/non-uniform is about space (\(\partial/\partial s\)). A nozzle flow at constant inlet conditions is steady (unchanging in time) but non-uniform (faster downstream). All four combinations are possible.

Rate of Flow

The quantity of fluid passing per unit time across a designated area is the flow rate. There are two versions: volume flow rate \(Q\) (how much volume per second) and mass flow rate \(\dot{m}\) (how much mass per second). These are the workhorses of the continuity equation coming up in Chapter 5.

Volume Flow Rate (uniform velocity)

If a fluid of velocity \(v\) crosses an area \(A\) at right angles, the volume that passes in time \(\Delta t\) is a slug of length \(\Delta x = v\,\Delta t\), so:

\[ Q = rac{\Delta V}{\Delta t} = rac{A\,\Delta x}{\Delta t} = A\,v \qquad \left[ frac{ ext{m}^3}{ ext{s}} ight] \]

\(Q\) — volume flow rate (m³/s) \(\Delta V\) — volume passing in \(\Delta t\) (m³) \(A\) — cross-sectional area (m²) \(v\) — velocity normal to the area (m/s)

When to use: Velocity is uniform across the section and perpendicular to it — the standard “pipe carrying speed v through area A” estimate.

When NOT to use: If velocity varies over the area (any real pipe profile) or is not normal to the area, you must integrate — see the general form below.

In time \(\Delta t\), the fluid crossing area \(A\) fills a slug of length \(v\,\Delta t\). Dividing that volume by \(\Delta t\) gives \(Q = Av\).
Volume Flow Rate (general)

In general the velocity is not uniform and the area may be tilted. For an area with outward unit normal \( ec{n}\), only the normal component of velocity \(v_n = ec{v}

5.1 — Reynolds Transport Theorem: Conservation of Mass

System → control volume • Extensive vs intensive properties • The RTT • Continuity equation • Worked examples: reservoir & jet engine

The Big Picture: Why We Need the RTT

Every fundamental law of mechanics — conservation of mass, Newton’s second law, conservation of energy — is written for a fixed lump of matter. In fluid mechanics we call that fixed lump a system: a fixed collection of atoms that we follow as it moves and deforms. This is the Lagrangian viewpoint, and it makes the laws easy to state:

The System Laws (Lagrangian form)
\[ \underbrace{ rac{dm}{dt} = 0}_{ ext{mass}} \qquad \underbrace{ ec F = rac{d}{dt}(m ec V)}_{ ext{linear momentum}} \qquad \underbrace{ ec M = rac{d}{dt}\!\int ( ec r imes ec V)\,dm}_{ ext{angular momentum}} \qquad \underbrace{\dot Q - \dot W = rac{dE}{dt}}_{ ext{energy}} \]

Each law tracks a property of one fixed mass as it travels through space. Exact, no averaging — but to use them we’d have to follow every fluid particle individually. For a flowing fluid that is hopeless.

What we actually care about in engineering is what happens at a fixed location in space — the thrust at a nozzle, the flow through a pump, the rise of water behind a dam. That is the Eulerian viewpoint: we draw a fixed region called a control volume (CV) and watch fluid stream in and out of it. The problem is that the laws above are written for systems, not for control volumes.

★ The Core Idea

The Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) is the bridge between the two viewpoints. It rewrites the rate of change of any system property as something we can evaluate entirely on a fixed control volume. Once we have it, we get continuity, the momentum equation, and the energy equation just by choosing which property to track.

System vs. Control Volume

Two Ways to Define Your “Stuff”

• A system (closed system) is a collection of matter with a fixed set of atoms. Mass is constant; the boundary moves and deforms with the fluid. Equations apply to individual masses and quantities are exact.

• A control volume (open system) is a selected region in space that fluid may flow into and out of. It can be fixed, move, or deform. Equations apply to a region and quantities are averaged over it. The CV is enclosed by a control surface (CS) — part real wall (pipe, nozzle), part imaginary (an inlet/outlet plane).

The classic mental image is a deodorant can. Treat the can plus the spray it ejects as a system (fixed mass, but it spreads everywhere — awkward to track). Or draw the CV as just the can itself: mass leaves through the nozzle, and we only track what crosses that surface. The CV is far more practical.

Control volumes come in three flavours, chosen to suit the problem:

Fixed CV

Locked in space. Use for nozzle/duct stress, pipe junctions. (e.g. nozzle reaction force)

Moving CV

Travels at constant velocity \( ec V_s\). Use for drag on a moving vehicle. (e.g. ship/aircraft drag)

Deforming CV

Boundary changes shape/size. Use for transient filling/emptying. (e.g. inflating balloon)

Recall: Extensive (B) vs. Intensive (β) Properties

To write one master equation that works for mass, momentum, and energy, we need generic symbols. Recall from §1.2 the distinction between extensive and intensive properties:

Generic Property and Its Per-Unit-Mass Value
\[ eta = rac{dB}{dm} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad B = \int_{ ext{sys}} eta\, ho\,d orall \]
\(B\) — any extensive property (scales with mass): total mass, momentum, or energy \(eta = dB/dm\) — the matching intensive property (the amount of \(B\) per unit mass) \( ho\) — fluid density [kg/m³] \(d orall\) — differential volume element [m³]

The whole power of the RTT is that we derive it once for the generic pair \((B,eta)\), then simply plug in:

Conservation law Extensive \(B\) Intensive \(eta = dB/dm\)
Mass (this lecture)\(m\)\(eta = m/m = 1\)
Linear momentum\(m ec V\)\(eta = ec V\)
Energy\(E\)\(eta = e = E/m\)

Recall: Flow Rate & Flux Through a Surface

Before deriving the theorem we need to count how much fluid crosses a surface per second. Consider a small patch of area \(dA\) with an outward unit normal \(\hat n\), through which fluid moves at velocity \( ec V\). In a time \(dt\) the fluid sweeps out a slanted slab. Only the velocity component along the normal moves fluid across the patch:

Figure 5.1.1 — Fluid crossing an area patch \(dA\). In time \(dt\) it sweeps the slanted slab of volume \(d orall = ( ec V

5.2 — Reynolds Transport Theorem: Linear Momentum

Newton’s 2nd law for a CV • Momentum equation • Steady-flow form • FBD approach • Moving CV • Four worked examples

Why Linear Momentum?

In Chapter 2 we computed forces on surfaces due to stationary fluids — hydrostatics. But what about a fire hose hitting a wall, a jet deflected by a vane, or water flowing under a sluice gate? These involve moving fluids that change velocity, and velocity changes require forces. The momentum equation lets us compute those forces without ever resolving the messy internal flow details — we only need what crosses the control surface.

★ Key Insight

The momentum equation is the most powerful problem-solving tool in this course. It replaces page-long pressure integrations with a simple bookkeeping exercise: draw a control volume, identify what flows in and out, and the forces fall out directly.

From Newton’s Second Law to the RTT

Recall from §5.1 that the RTT rewrites the rate of change of any extensive system property \(B\) in terms of a control volume. For linear momentum we set:

Momentum as the Extensive Property
\[ B = m\vec{V} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \beta = \frac{dB}{dm} = \vec{V} \]
\(B = m\vec{V}\) — total linear momentum of the system (kg·m/s) \(\beta = \vec{V}\) — velocity = momentum per unit mass (m/s)

Newton’s second law for a system (fixed collection of matter) says:

Newton’s Second Law (System Form)
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{external}} = \frac{d(m\vec{V})}{dt}\bigg|_{\text{system}} \]
\(\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\) — vector sum of all external forces on the system \(d(m\vec{V})/dt\) — rate of change of the system’s momentum

This is valid only for a system — a fixed mass. To apply it to a control volume (where mass flows in and out), we substitute \(\beta = \vec{V}\) into the general RTT from §5.1:

The Linear Momentum Equation

Linear Momentum Equation (General Form)
\[ \boxed{\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{\text{CV}} \vec{V}\,\rho\;d\forall \;+\; \int_{\text{CS}} \vec{V}\,\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\;dA} \]
\(\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\) — sum of all external forces acting on the contents of the CV \(\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\int_{\text{CV}} \vec{V}\,\rho\;d\forall\) — local (storage) term: rate of change of momentum stored inside the CV \(\displaystyle\int_{\text{CS}} \vec{V}\,\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\;dA\) — convective (flux) term: net momentum carried out through the CS \(\hat{n}\) — outward unit normal on the control surface
★ Three-Term Interpretation

Read the equation left to right: “Forces on the CV = rate the momentum inside the CV is growing + rate momentum is being carried out.” The LHS is forces (draw a free-body diagram). The first RHS term is zero for steady flow. The second RHS term is the momentum flux.

Steady-Flow Simplification

For steady flow (\(\partial/\partial t = 0\) everywhere), the storage term vanishes. Nothing inside the CV is changing with time — the same pattern repeats each instant:

Steady-Flow Linear Momentum
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \int_{\text{CS}} \vec{V}\,\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\;dA \]
Steady flow ⇒ storage term = 0 Only the momentum flux through the CS remains

If the flow is also incompressible and inviscid (ideal), the velocity is uniform across each inlet and outlet. The integral collapses to a sum over discrete ports:

Steady Ideal Flow — Discrete Form
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \sum_{\text{ports}} \vec{V}\,\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,A \]
Each port contributes one term: the velocity vector \(\vec{V}\) times the mass flow rate \(\rho(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})A\) At an inlet: \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n} < 0\) (flow opposes outward normal) ⇒ negative contribution At an outlet: \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n} > 0\) (flow aligns with outward normal) ⇒ positive contribution

Tackling the Right-Hand Side (Momentum Flux)

Resolve the momentum equation into scalar x- and y-components. For each component, the flux term becomes:

x-Component Example
\[ \overset{+}{\rightarrow}\;\sum F_x = \sum V_x\;\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,A = (V_{\text{in}})_x\underbrace{(-\rho V_{\text{in}} A_{\text{in}})}_{\dot{m}_{\text{in}}} + (V_{\text{out}})_x\underbrace{(\rho V_{\text{out}} A_{\text{out}})}_{\dot{m}_{\text{out}}} \]
\(V_x\) — the x-component of the velocity at each port (carries the sign from geometry) \(\rho V A\) — the mass flow rate at each port (always positive as a magnitude) The sign of \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n}\) handles inlet vs outlet automatically: negative at inlets, positive at outlets
★ Pay Attention to Signs

There are two velocity appearances in each term: \(\vec{V}\) outside (gives the direction of momentum) and \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n}\) inside (gives the sign of mass flow). The first carries component signs from geometry. The second is negative at inlets (flow opposes the outward normal) and positive at outlets.

Tackling the Left-Hand Side (Free-Body Diagram)

The left-hand side is the vector sum of all external forces on the control volume. Start every problem by drawing a free-body diagram (FBD) of the CV:

External Forces on a CV
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \vec{F}_{\text{pressure}} + \vec{F}_{\text{weight}} + \vec{F}_{\text{normal}} + \vec{F}_{\text{shear}} \]
\(\vec{F}_{\text{pressure}}\) — pressure forces at each inlet/outlet (push fluid into the CV) \(\vec{F}_{\text{weight}}\) — gravity (= \(W\) downward, often negligible for horizontal gas flows) \(\vec{F}_{\text{normal}}\) — support reactions from walls, flanges, bolts \(\vec{F}_{\text{shear}}\) — friction along walls (zero for inviscid/ideal flow assumptions)

Resolve these into x- and y-components and handle each direction independently. For many problems (jets hitting surfaces, nozzle reactions), pressure forces at open inlets/outlets to atmosphere are zero (gage pressure = 0), and for ideal flow shear forces are zero — leaving only the reaction force you’re solving for.

Free-body diagram of a curved duct CV: pressure forces at inlet/outlet, weight, normal reaction, and shear.
★ Why Momentum Is So Powerful

The momentum equation computes forces without resolving the details inside the CV. You could calculate the same result by integrating \(p \cdot dA\) and \(\tau \cdot dA\) around every surface inside the duct — but that would be enormously tedious. The momentum approach needs only the conditions at the inlets and outlets.

Oversimplified Form (One Inlet, One Outlet)

For the special case of steady, uniform, non-moving CV with one inlet and one outlet, the general equation collapses to:

Simplified Momentum (Single Inlet/Outlet)
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \vec{v}_{\text{out}}\,\dot{m}_{\text{out}} - \vec{v}_{\text{in}}\,\dot{m}_{\text{in}} \]
\(\vec{v}_{\text{out}}\) — velocity vector at the outlet \(\vec{v}_{\text{in}}\) — velocity vector at the inlet \(\dot{m}_{\text{out}} = \rho V_{\text{out}} A_{\text{out}}\), \(\dot{m}_{\text{in}} = \rho V_{\text{in}} A_{\text{in}}\) — mass flow rates
★ Exam Warning

This simplified form works for simple one-inlet/one-outlet problems, but it is easy to make sign errors when there are multiple outlets, angled flows, or moving CVs. Dr. Bano recommends using the full formulas with the \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n}\) sign convention for anything beyond the simplest cases. The full form handles signs automatically.

Problem-Solving Strategy

Momentum Problem Checklist

Step 1: Draw the CV and CS. Mark all inlets and outlets. Choose a coordinate system.

Step 2: Draw the FBD of the CV. Include pressure forces, weight, reaction forces, and shear (if viscous).

Step 3: Write continuity (\(\dot{m}_{\text{in}} = \dot{m}_{\text{out}}\)) to relate velocities and areas.

Step 4: Write the momentum equation in x and y components. Evaluate the \(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n}\) dot product at each port (negative at inlets, positive at outlets).

Step 5: Substitute known values and solve for the unknown forces.

Example 1: Fire Hose Hitting a Fixed Surface

Example — Fire Hose Splitting Flow

Water is discharged from a 1 in diameter nozzle at 180 gal/min. The flow strikes a fixed surface such that ¾ flows along path B (straight down, −y), while ¼ flows along path C (at 60° from the positive x-axis). The nozzle enters at 45° below the positive x-axis. Determine the x- and y-components of the resultant force on the surface. Assume ideal steady flow. \(\gamma_{\text{water}} = 62.4\;\text{lbf/ft}^3\).

CV around the deflecting surface: inlet A (45° below +x), outlet B (straight down), outlet C (60° above +x).
Solution

Step 1 — Flow rates and velocities.

Convert the discharge:

\[ Q_A = \frac{180\;\text{gal}}{\text{min}} \times \frac{1\;\text{min}}{60\;\text{s}} \times \frac{1\;\text{ft}^3}{7.48\;\text{gal}} = 0.4011\;\text{ft}^3/\text{s} \]

Nozzle area and velocity at A (diameter = 1 in = 1/12 ft):

\[ A_A = \pi\!\left(\frac{0.5}{12}\right)^{\!2} = 5.454 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{ft}^2 \] \[ V_A = \frac{Q_A}{A_A} = \frac{0.4011}{5.454 \times 10^{-3}} = 73.53\;\text{ft/s} \]

Flow splits: \(Q_B = \tfrac{3}{4}Q_A = 0.3008\;\text{ft}^3/\text{s}\), \(Q_C = \tfrac{1}{4}Q_A = 0.1003\;\text{ft}^3/\text{s}\).

For ideal flow (no friction losses), Bernoulli along each streamline from A → B and A → C with atmospheric pressure everywhere gives \(V_B = V_C = V_A = 73.53\;\text{ft/s}\).

Density: \(\rho = \gamma/g = 62.4/32.2 = 1.938\;\text{slug/ft}^3\).

Step 2 — Momentum equation, x-component.

Select CV around the surface. For steady ideal flow:

\[ \overset{+}{\rightarrow}\;\sum F_x = \sum V_x\;\rho\,(\vec{V}\cdot\hat{n})\,A \]

Evaluate each port. The inlet flow direction is at \(-45°\) (below the +x axis):

\[ -F_x = \underbrace{Q_B V_B \cos(-90°)}_{=\;0} + Q_C V_C \cos(60°) - Q_A V_A \cos(-45°) \] \[ -F_x = 0 + (0.1003)(73.53)\cos 60° - (0.4011)(73.53)\cos 45° \] \[ -F_x = 3.69 - 20.86 = -17.17 \]

Wait — let me redo this more carefully using the \(\rho\) factor. Each flux term is \(V_x \cdot \rho \cdot Q\):

\[ -F_x = \rho\bigl[Q_B V_B \cos(-90°) + Q_C V_C \cos(60°) - Q_A V_A \cos(45°)\bigr] \] \[ = 1.938\bigl[0 + (0.1003)(73.53)(0.5) - (0.4011)(73.53)(0.7071)\bigr] \] \[ = 1.938\bigl[3.688 - 20.86\bigr] = 1.938(-17.17) = -33.3\;\text{lb} \] \[ \boxed{F_x = 33.3\;\text{lb} \;\leftarrow} \]

Step 3 — y-component.

\[ F_y = \rho\bigl[Q_B V_B \sin(-90°) + Q_C V_C \sin(60°) - Q_A V_A \sin(-45°)\bigr] \] \[ = 1.938\bigl[(0.3008)(73.53)(-1) + (0.1003)(73.53)(0.8660) - (0.4011)(73.53)(-0.7071)\bigr] \] \[ = 1.938\bigl[-22.12 + 6.389 + 20.86\bigr] = 1.938(5.12) = 9.92\;\text{lb} \] \[ \boxed{F_y = 9.92\;\text{lb} \;\uparrow} \]

Resultant:

\[ |\vec{F}| = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{33.3^2 + 9.92^2} = \boxed{34.7\;\text{lb}} \]

Moving Control Volume at Constant Velocity

When the CV moves at a constant velocity \(\vec{V}_b\) (e.g. the CV is attached to a truck, boat, or vane), the momentum equation still holds but all velocities must be relative to the CV:

Steady Ideal Flow — Moving CV
\[ \sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = \sum \vec{V}_{f/b}\;\rho\,(\vec{V}_{f/b}\cdot\hat{n})\,A \]
\(\vec{V}_{f/b} = \vec{V}_{\text{flow}} - \vec{V}_b\) — velocity of the fluid relative to the body/CV \(\vec{V}_{\text{flow}}\) — absolute velocity of the fluid (in the lab frame) \(\vec{V}_b\) — velocity of the body/CV (constant)
★ Relative Velocity Rule

Replace every \(\vec{V}\) in the momentum equation with \(\vec{V}_{f/b}\). The forces remain in the absolute frame (they don’t change), but the momentum fluxes are computed with the relative velocity because the CV’s mass flow depends on how fast the fluid enters/leaves relative to the moving surface.

Example 2: Force on a Windshield (Moving CV)

Example — Hose Hitting a Moving Truck

A hose with nozzle diameter \(D = 50\;\text{mm}\) discharges water at \(Q = 8\;\text{L/s}\). The stream hits the windshield of a truck moving at \(5\;\text{m/s}\) toward the hose. The deflected stream leaves at \(40°\) above the horizontal. Determine the force on the windshield. Assume steady ideal flow; \(\rho = 1000\;\text{kg/m}^3\).

Solution

Step 1 — Absolute velocity of the jet.

\[ V = \frac{Q}{\pi D^2/4} = \frac{8 \times 10^{-3}}{\pi(0.05)^2/4} = 4.074\;\text{m/s} \]

Step 2 — Relative velocity. Attach the CV to the truck (moving left at 5 m/s). The jet moves right at 4.074 m/s. In the truck’s frame:

\[ V_{f/A} = V_{\text{flow}} - V_b = 4.074 - (-5) = 9.074\;\text{m/s} \]

(The truck moves at \(-5\) m/s in our sign convention since it heads toward the hose.)

For ideal flow with equal inlet and outlet areas, \(V_{f/B} = V_{f/A} = 9.074\;\text{m/s}\).

Step 3 — x-momentum (moving CV).

\[ \sum F_x = V_{f/B}\cos 40°\;(\rho V_{f/B} A_B) - V_{f/A}\;(\rho V_{f/A} A_A) \]

With \(A_A = A_B = \pi(0.025)^2 = 1.9635 \times 10^{-3}\;\text{m}^2\):

\[ \sum F_x = (9.074\cos 40°)(1000)(9.074)(1.9635\times10^{-3}) - (9.074)(1000)(9.074)(1.9635\times10^{-3}) \] \[ = \rho\,V_{f}^{2}\,A\,(\cos 40° - 1) = (1000)(9.074)^2(1.9635\times10^{-3})(0.766 - 1) \] \[ = 161.7 \times (-0.234) = -37.83\;\text{N} \] \[ \boxed{F_x = 37.83\;\text{N}\;\leftarrow} \]

Step 4 — y-momentum.

\[ \sum F_y = V_{f/B}\sin 40°\;(\rho V_{f/B} A_B) = \rho\,V_{f}^{2}\,A\,\sin 40° \] \[ = (1000)(9.074)^2(1.9635\times10^{-3})(0.6428) = 103.9\;\text{N} \] \[ \boxed{F_y = 103.9\;\text{N}\;\uparrow} \]

Resultant:

\[ |\vec{F}| = \sqrt{37.83^2 + 103.9^2} = \boxed{111\;\text{N}} \]

Example 3: Concrete Flowing Into a Cart

Example — Cable Tension and Scale Reading

Concrete flows into a cart sitting on a scale. The concrete stream has density \(\rho = 1700\;\text{kg/m}^3\), cross-sectional area \(A = 0.12\;\text{m}^2\), and speed \(v_1 = 3\;\text{m/s}\), entering at angle \(\alpha = 60°\) below the horizontal. The cart plus concrete weighs \(W = 3600\;\text{N}\). Determine the tension in the cable and the weight recorded by the scale. Assume steady flow.

CV around the cart: concrete enters at angle α = 60°. FBD shows cable tension T, weight W, and normal force N from the scale.
Solution

The CV encloses the cart and concrete. There is one inlet (the stream) and no outlet (concrete accumulates, but we assume steady flow at this instant).

x-momentum:

\[ \sum F_x = \sum_{\text{CS}} v_x\;\rho\;\vec{v}\cdot\vec{A} \]

The only CS flux is at the inlet. The stream enters at angle \(\alpha = 60°\) below horizontal, so \(v_{1x} = v_1\cos\alpha\), and the dot product \(\vec{v}\cdot\hat{n}\) is \(-v_1\) (flow into the CV):

\[ T = -v_{1x} \cdot \rho \cdot v_1 \cdot A_1 = -v_1\cos\alpha \cdot \rho v_1 A_1 = -\rho A_1 v_1^2 \cos\alpha \] \[ T = -(1700)(0.12)(3)^2\cos 60° = -(1700)(0.12)(9)(0.5) = -918\;\text{N} \]

The negative sign means T acts opposite to our assumed direction — the cable is in tension (pulls the cart to the right, resisting the horizontal momentum of the incoming stream).

\[ \boxed{T = 918\;\text{N (tension)}} \]

y-momentum:

\[ N - W = +v_{1y}\;\rho\;v_1\;A_1 \]

The stream enters with a downward vertical component \(v_{1y} = -v_1\sin\alpha\), so the flux brings downward momentum into the CV:

\[ N - W = -(-v_1\sin\alpha)(\rho v_1 A_1) = +\rho A_1 v_1^2 \sin\alpha \]

Wait — let me be careful. The dot product at the inlet is \(\vec{v}\cdot\hat{n} = -v_1\) (inflow), so the y-flux is \(v_{1y}(-\rho v_1 A_1)\). With \(v_{1y} = -v_1 \sin\alpha\) (downward):

\[ N - W = (-v_1\sin\alpha)(-\rho v_1 A_1) = \rho A_1 v_1^2 \sin\alpha \] \[ N = W + \rho A_1 v_1^2 \sin\alpha = 3600 + (1700)(0.12)(9)\sin 60° = 3600 + 1590 = 5190\;\text{N} \] \[ \boxed{N = 5190\;\text{N} \;\text{(scale reads 5190 N)}} \]

The scale reads more than the weight because it also supports the downward momentum of the incoming concrete stream.

Example 4: Force on a Sluice Gate

Example — Sluice Gate with Bernoulli + Momentum

When sluice gate G is open, water flows out from under the gate at a depth of 2 ft. The gate is 5 ft wide. The channel behind the gate maintains a constant depth of 10 ft. Determine the horizontal force that must be applied to the gate to keep it in place. Assume ideal steady flow. \(\gamma = 62.4\;\text{lbf/ft}^3\).

Sluice gate: upstream depth 10 ft, downstream depth 2 ft, gate 5 ft wide. Bernoulli between ① and ② gives velocities; momentum gives the gate force.
Solution

This problem combines Bernoulli (to find velocities) with the momentum equation (to find the gate force). It also uses hydrostatics for the pressure forces on the CV faces.

Step 1 — Bernoulli between ① and ②.

Both free surfaces are at atmospheric pressure (\(p_1 = p_2 = 0\) gage). Take the datum at the channel bed:

\[ \frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_A^2}{2g} + z_1 = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_B^2}{2g} + z_2 \] \[ 0 + \frac{V_A^2}{2(32.2)} + 10 = 0 + \frac{V_B^2}{2(32.2)} + 2 \] \[ V_B^2 - V_A^2 = 2(32.2)(8) = 515.2\;\text{(ft/s)}^2 \]

Step 2 — Continuity.

Width \(w = 5\;\text{ft}\). Areas: \(A_A = 10 \times 5 = 50\;\text{ft}^2\), \(A_B = 2 \times 5 = 10\;\text{ft}^2\).

\[ \rho A_A V_A = \rho A_B V_B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 50\,V_A = 10\,V_B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_B = 5\,V_A \]

Step 3 — Solve for velocities.

Substitute \(V_B = 5V_A\) into Bernoulli:

\[ (5V_A)^2 - V_A^2 = 515.2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 24\,V_A^2 = 515.2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_A = 4.633\;\text{ft/s} \] \[ V_B = 5(4.633) = 23.17\;\text{ft/s} \]

Step 4 — Free-body diagram and momentum.

The CV encloses the water between section A and section B. External forces in the x-direction:

• \(F_A\) = hydrostatic force on upstream face = \(\frac{1}{2}\gamma h_A^2 w = \frac{1}{2}(62.4)(10)^2(5) = 15{,}600\;\text{lb}\) (pushing right)

• \(F_B\) = hydrostatic force on downstream face = \(\frac{1}{2}\gamma h_B^2 w = \frac{1}{2}(62.4)(2)^2(5) = 624\;\text{lb}\) (pushing left)

• \(F_G\) = force from the gate (pushing left, unknown)

x-momentum:

\[ \overset{+}{\rightarrow}\;\sum F_x = V_B(\rho V_B A_B) - V_A(\rho V_A A_A) \] \[ F_A - F_G - F_B = \rho(V_B^2 A_B - V_A^2 A_A) \]

With \(\rho = 62.4/32.2 = 1.938\;\text{slug/ft}^3\):

\[ \rho V_B^2 A_B = 1.938(23.17)^2(10) = 10{,}404\;\text{lb} \] \[ \rho V_A^2 A_A = 1.938(4.633)^2(50) = 2{,}080\;\text{lb} \] \[ 15{,}600 - F_G - 624 = 10{,}404 - 2{,}080 = 8{,}324 \] \[ F_G = 15{,}600 - 624 - 8{,}324 = \boxed{6{,}652\;\text{lb}} \]

(The small difference from the slide value of 6656 lb is due to rounding in intermediate steps.)

★ Sluice Gate Pattern

Sluice gate problems always combine three tools: (1) Bernoulli to relate velocities, (2) continuity to get velocities from depths, (3) momentum to find the gate force. The pressure forces on the CV faces come from hydrostatics (triangular pressure distributions). Watch for this pattern on the exam.

    plugging directly into equations — convert: ρ = SG × ρ_W first.

    Dimensionless density ratio. Reference: water at 4°C.

    Newton's Law of Viscosity #4
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{\tau} = \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\mu} \frac{d\textcolor{#E65100}{u}}{d\textcolor{#1565C0}{y}} \]

    Shear stress is proportional to velocity gradient. The constant μ is the dynamic viscosity.

    ✓ Use when
    finding shear force on plates, determining viscosity from experiment, pipe flow wall shear.
    ✗ Not for
    non-Newtonian fluids (variable μ). Not for turbulent flow.

    Shear stress = viscosity × velocity gradient. Newtonian fluids only.

    Kinematic Viscosity #5
    \[ \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\nu} = \frac{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\mu}}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}} \]

    Dynamic viscosity normalized by density. Has dimensions of diffusivity (m²/s).

    ✓ Use when
    Reynolds number: Re = VL/ν. Comparing fluids of different densities.
    ✗ Not for
    finding shear stress — need μ for that (τ = μ du/dy).

    Viscosity normalized by density. Used in Reynolds number.

    Droplet / Bubble Pressure #6
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{\Delta p} = \frac{2\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\Upsilon}}{\textcolor{#E65100}{R}} \;\text{(droplet)} \qquad \frac{4\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\Upsilon}}{\textcolor{#E65100}{R}} \;\text{(bubble)} \]

    Surface tension creates internal pressure. Bubbles have two surfaces → 2× droplet pressure.

    ✓ Use when
    pressure inside droplets, bubbles, or curved menisci.
    ✗ Not for
    non-spherical geometries. Gravity effects neglected.

    Pressure excess inside curved surfaces from surface tension.

    Capillary Height #7
    \[ \textcolor{#1565C0}{h} = \frac{2\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\Upsilon} \textcolor{#7B1FA2}{\cos\theta}}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\gamma} \, \textcolor{#E65100}{R}} \]

    Height a liquid rises or falls in a narrow tube. Positive for wetting (θ < 90°), negative for non-wetting.

    ✓ Use when
    capillary tube problems, correcting manometer readings in small tubes.
    ✗ Not for
    non-circular tubes. Requires known θ and Υ.

    Capillary rise. Positive = wetting, negative = non-wetting.

    Ideal Gas Law #8
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p} = \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho} \, \textcolor{#E65100}{R} \, \textcolor{#E65100}{T} \]

    Equation of state for ideal gases — relates absolute pressure, density, and absolute temperature.

    ✓ Use when
    gas density at given conditions, compressible flow, atmosphere problems.
    ✗ Not for
    very high p or low T (real gas). Must use absolute p and T — never gauge or °C.

    Ideal gas EOS. Use absolute pressure (Pa) and temperature (K).

    Absolute / Gage Pressure #9
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_{\text{abs}}} = \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_{\text{gage}}} + \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_{\text{atm}}} \]

    Absolute = total from vacuum. Gage = above atmospheric. Vacuum = below atmospheric.

    ✓ Use when
    converting gage ↔ absolute, ideal gas law (needs absolute p).
    ✗ Not for
    p_gage can be negative (vacuum). p_abs is never negative.

    Absolute = gage + atmospheric. p_atm ≈ 101.325 kPa.

    Hydrostatic Pressure #10
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p} = \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_a} + \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\gamma} \, \textcolor{#1565C0}{h} \]

    Pressure increases linearly with depth in a static incompressible fluid.

    ✓ Use when
    pressure at depth, manometer analysis, pressure on submerged surfaces.
    ✗ Not for
    compressible fluids (γ varies). Not for moving fluids.

    Pressure at depth h. Linear in incompressible fluid.

    Manometer Equation #11
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_A} - \textcolor{#D32F2F}{p_B} = \sum \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\gamma_i} \, \textcolor{#1565C0}{\Delta h_i} \]

    Walk A→B through manometer: go down → add γΔh, go up → subtract γΔh.

    ✓ Use when
    pressure difference via U-tube or multi-fluid manometer.
    ✗ Not for
    dynamic flows. Down adds pressure, up subtracts.

    Walk through: +γΔh down, −γΔh up.

    Ch 2 — Hydrostatic Forces & Buoyancy

    Resultant Hydrostatic Force #12
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{F_R} = \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\gamma} \, \textcolor{#1565C0}{\bar{h}} \, \textcolor{#1565C0}{A} \]

    Total force on a submerged plane surface = pressure at centroid × area.

    ✓ Use when
    total force on a gate, dam, tank wall, or any flat submerged surface.
    ✗ Not for
    curved surfaces (project onto planes). \(\bar{h}\) is vertical depth, not along surface.

    Resultant force = pressure at centroid × area.

    Center of Pressure #13
    \[ \textcolor{#1565C0}{y_{cp}} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{\bar{y}} + \frac{\textcolor{#00838F}{I_{xx}}}{\textcolor{#1565C0}{\bar{y}} \, \textcolor{#1565C0}{A}} \]

    Center of pressure is always below the centroid. Offset I_xx/(ȳA) is always positive.

    ✓ Use when
    finding where F_R acts — needed for moment/equilibrium on gates, hinges.
    ✗ Not for
    \(\bar{y}\) is along the incline from free-surface line, not vertical. Use centroidal I_xx.

    Center of pressure = centroid + offset. Always below centroid.

    Ch 3 — Bernoulli’s Equation

    Bernoulli Equation (energy form) #14
    \[ \frac{\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P}}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}} + \frac{\textcolor{#E65100}{V}^2}{2} + \textcolor{#2E7D32}{g}\,\textcolor{#1565C0}{z} = \text{const} \]

    Mechanical energy per unit mass is conserved along a streamline for steady, incompressible, frictionless flow. Each term has units of J/kg.

    ✓ Use when
    relating pressure, speed and height between two points on the same streamline — tanks, nozzles, ideal flow.
    ✗ Not for
    viscous/frictional flow, pumps or turbines (shaft work), unsteady or compressible flow, or jumping across streamlines.

    P/ρ + V²/2 + gz is constant along a streamline (steady, inviscid, incompressible).

    Bernoulli Equation (head form) #15
    \[ \frac{\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P}}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#2E7D32}{g}} + \frac{\textcolor{#E65100}{V}^2}{2\textcolor{#2E7D32}{g}} + \textcolor{#1565C0}{z} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{H} \]

    The energy form divided by g — every term now has units of metres (head). P/(ρg) is the pressure head, V²/(2g) the velocity head, z the elevation head. Note ρg = γ, the specific weight.

    ✓ Use when
    working with the EGL/HGL, pump or turbine head, or manometer heights where metres are the natural unit.
    ✗ Not for
    same limits as the energy form — no friction, no shaft work, one streamline only.

    Pressure head + velocity head + elevation head = total head H (constant along a streamline).

    Steady-Flow Euler Equation #16
    \[ d\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P} + \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{V}\,d\textcolor{#E65100}{V} + \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#2E7D32}{g}\,d\textcolor{#1565C0}{z} = 0 \]

    The differential form of Bernoulli before integration — Newton’s second law along a streamline for an inviscid fluid. Integrating along the streamline yields the Bernoulli equation.

    ✓ Use when
    deriving Bernoulli, or reasoning about the pressure gradient along a streamline.
    ✗ Not for
    a plug-and-play formula — it is the starting differential relation, not an algebraic result.

    dP + ρV·dV + ρg·dz = 0 — integrate to recover Bernoulli.

    Stagnation Pressure #17
    \[ \textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_0} = \textcolor{#D32F2F}{P} + \tfrac{1}{2}\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{V}^2 \]

    Pressure at a point where the flow is brought isentropically to rest: static pressure P plus dynamic pressure ½ρV². This is the basis of Pitot-tube velocity measurement.

    ✓ Use when
    relating total, static and dynamic pressure; finding speed from a Pitot or stagnation tube.
    ✗ Not for
    high-speed compressible flow (needs a compressibility correction) — the dynamic term assumes incompressible flow.

    P₀ = P + ½ρV². Stagnation = static + dynamic pressure.

    Continuity (incompressible) #18
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{Q} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{A_1}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{V_1} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{A_2}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{V_2} \]

    For steady incompressible flow the volume flow rate Q is constant, so a smaller area forces a faster velocity. Paired with Bernoulli for every flow-measurement device.

    ✓ Use when
    relating velocities at two pipe sections, or computing Q from area and speed.
    ✗ Not for
    compressible flow (use mass flow ρAV) or unsteady flow with storage.

    Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. Area down → velocity up.

    Pitot / Stagnation Tube Velocity #19
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{V_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_0} - \textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_1}\right)}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}}} \]

    The stagnation relation rearranged for speed — from the difference between stagnation and static pressure. A Pitot-static tube senses both pressures at once.

    ✓ Use when
    finding flow speed from a Pitot or Pitot-static probe reading.
    ✗ Not for
    compressible flow without correction, or a misaligned (yawed) probe.

    V = √(2(P₀ − P₁)/ρ). Speed from stagnation minus static pressure.

    Venturi Meter Flow Rate #20
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{Q} = C_v\,\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_2}\sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_1} - \textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_2}\right)}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\left(1 - (\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_2}/\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_1})^2\right)}} \]

    Bernoulli plus continuity across a smooth contraction. The velocity coefficient C_v (≈ 0.98) corrects for small friction losses; the gentle shape gives nearly full pressure recovery.

    ✓ Use when
    metering pipe flow with a Venturi; take C_v from calibration or charts.
    ✗ Not for
    very low Reynolds number (C_v drops), or using the pipe area — A₂ is the throat.

    Q = C_v A₂ √(2(P₁−P₂) / [ρ(1−(A₂/A₁)²)]). C_v ≈ 0.98.

    Orifice Meter Flow Rate #21
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{Q} = C_D\,\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_0}\sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(\textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_1} - \textcolor{#D32F2F}{P_2}\right)}{\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\left(1 - C_c^2(\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_0}/\textcolor{#1565C0}{A_1})^2\right)}} \]

    Same principle as the Venturi but with a sharp-edged plate. The jet necks down to a vena contracta (C_c ≈ 0.6), and the discharge coefficient C_D = C_c·C_v bundles contraction and friction. Cheaper than a Venturi but with a larger permanent pressure loss; a bell-mouth inlet has C_c = 1.

    ✓ Use when
    metering pipe flow with an orifice plate; take C_D from standards or calibration.
    ✗ Not for
    cases needing low pressure loss (use a Venturi), or forgetting contraction — the area is the hole A₀, the jet is smaller.

    Q = C_D A₀ √(2(P₁−P₂) / [ρ(1−C_c²(A₀/A₁)²)]). C_c ≈ 0.6, C_D = C_c·C_v.

    Ch 4 — Introduction to Fluid Dynamics

    Velocity Field #22
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{\vec{V}} = \textcolor{#E65100}{u}\,\vec{i} + \textcolor{#E65100}{v}\,\vec{j} + \textcolor{#E65100}{w}\,\vec{k} \]

    The Eulerian velocity field — velocity as a function of position and time, carried by three scalar components.

    ✓ Use when
    describing flow at fixed points in space, or locating a stagnation point (set V⃗ = 0 and solve).
    ✗ Not for
    tracking a single particle over time — that is the Lagrangian description.

    Velocity as a field: components u, v, w at each point.

    Volume Flow Rate #23
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{Q} = \int_A \textcolor{#E65100}{v_n}\,dA = \textcolor{#E65100}{\bar{U}}\,\textcolor{#1565C0}{A} \]

    Volume per unit time through a section. Only the velocity normal to the area carries flow — integrate it, or use average velocity × area.

    ✓ Use when
    finding discharge through a pipe or duct from a velocity profile or a known Ū.
    ✗ Not for
    mass flow of a compressible fluid — multiply by ρ (see #25). Tangential velocity adds nothing.

    Q = ∫vₙ dA = Ū·A. Normal velocity only.

    Average Velocity #24
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{\bar{U}} = \dfrac{\textcolor{#E65100}{Q}}{\textcolor{#1565C0}{A}} \]

    The single uniform velocity that carries the same discharge Q through the area — collapses a velocity profile to one number.

    ✓ Use when
    reducing a profile to a representative speed; Reynolds number, head loss, continuity.
    ✗ Not for
    the peak/centerline velocity — for laminar pipe flow Ū = V_max/2, not V_max.

    Ū = Q/A. Profile collapsed to one speed.

    Mass Flow Rate #25
    \[ \textcolor{#E65100}{\dot{m}} = \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{Q} = \textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,\textcolor{#E65100}{\bar{U}}\,\textcolor{#1565C0}{A} \]

    Mass per unit time = density × volume flow. The form that conserves across a control volume even when area or velocity changes.

    ✓ Use when
    conservation of mass / continuity, compressible flow, mixing and energy balances.
    ✗ Not for
    incompressible volume continuity — there Q is conserved; ṁ simply adds the ρ factor.

    ṁ = ρQ = ρŪA. Mass per unit time.

    Ch 5 — Reynolds Transport Theorem

    Linear Momentum Equation (General) #26
    \[ \sum \textcolor{#E65100}{\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\int_{\text{CV}} \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}}\,\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\;d\forall \;+\; \int_{\text{CS}} \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}}\,\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,(\textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}}\!\cdot\!\textcolor{#9C27B0}{\hat{n}})\;dA \]

    The RTT applied to linear momentum. Left side = external forces. First integral = rate of momentum change stored inside the CV (zero for steady flow). Second integral = net momentum flux through the control surface.

    ✓ Use when
    finding forces on ducts, nozzles, vanes, gates, or any surface interacting with fluid; works for steady or unsteady, uniform or non-uniform flow.
    ✗ Not for
    non-inertial (accelerating) CVs — use the modified form with apparent forces. Also not for angular momentum — that needs the moment-of-momentum equation.

    ΣF⃗ = ∂/∂t ∫ V⃗ρ dV + ∫ V⃗ρ(V⃗·n̂) dA. General form; drop storage term for steady flow.

    Steady Ideal Flow Momentum #27
    \[ \sum \textcolor{#E65100}{\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}} = \sum_{\text{ports}} \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}}\,\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,(\textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}}\!\cdot\!\textcolor{#9C27B0}{\hat{n}})\,\textcolor{#D32F2F}{A} \]

    Steady + incompressible + inviscid (ideal) flow with uniform velocity at each port. The integral collapses to a sum over discrete inlets and outlets. V⃗·n̂ is negative at inlets, positive at outlets.

    ✓ Use when
    flow is steady, ideal, and uniform at each port — most MAAE 2300 problems; multiple inlets/outlets handled naturally.
    ✗ Not for
    unsteady filling/emptying problems or non-uniform velocity profiles — go back to the integral form #26.

    ΣF⃗ = Σ V⃗ρ(V⃗·n̂)A. Discrete-port form; V⃗·n̂ < 0 at inlets.

    Simplified Momentum (1-in / 1-out) #28
    \[ \sum \textcolor{#E65100}{\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{v}_{\text{out}}}\,\textcolor{#D32F2F}{\dot{m}_{\text{out}}} - \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{v}_{\text{in}}}\,\textcolor{#D32F2F}{\dot{m}_{\text{in}}} \]

    The simplest form: steady, uniform, non-moving CV with exactly one inlet and one outlet. Each velocity carries its own directional sign from geometry. Prone to sign errors for angled flows.

    ✓ Use when
    simple one-inlet/one-outlet problems with a stationary CV (e.g. pipe bend, nozzle reaction).
    ✗ Not for
    multiple outlets/inlets (use #27), moving CVs (use #29), or problems where sign confusion is likely — the full form is safer.

    ΣF⃗ = v⃗_out·ṁ_out − v⃗_in·ṁ_in. One inlet, one outlet, stationary CV.

    Moving CV Momentum #29
    \[ \sum \textcolor{#E65100}{\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}} = \sum \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}_{f/b}}\;\textcolor{#2E7D32}{\rho}\,(\textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}_{f/b}}\!\cdot\!\hat{n})\,\textcolor{#D32F2F}{A} \quad\text{where}\quad \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}_{f/b}} = \textcolor{#1565C0}{\vec{V}_{\text{flow}}} - \textcolor{#9C27B0}{\vec{V}_b} \]

    When the CV moves at constant velocity V⃗_b, replace every velocity with the relative velocity V⃗_f/b. The forces remain in the absolute frame. The relative velocity determines the mass flow rate crossing the CS.

    ✓ Use when
    the CV is attached to a moving object (truck, boat, turbine blade) at constant speed.
    ✗ Not for
    accelerating CVs — those need the non-inertial modification with an extra −a_CV ∫ρ dV term.

    ΣF⃗ = Σ V⃗_f/b ρ(V⃗_f/b·n̂)A. V⃗_f/b = V⃗_flow − V⃗_b. Relative velocity everywhere.

    💡 Insider Tips

    • Every long-answer starts with a CV sketch. Draw the control volume, label all inlets/outlets, show pressure forces and the reaction force you're solving for. Partial marks come from this.
    • Bernoulli + Continuity are always paired. You'll never use Bernoulli alone — continuity gives you the velocity relationship, then Bernoulli connects pressures/elevations.
    • Hydrostatic pressure on a vertical surface = ρg·yc·A. The centroid depth yc is at half the water height. This substitution appears in every momentum problem involving open-channel flow.
    • Sign convention matters. Pick a positive direction, define FR as the force on the fluid (not the gate), then flip at the end. Getting this backwards is the #1 error.
    • Mass conservation ≠ volume conservation. Q1c proves this — the air and water have different densities, so equal volume flow rates give very different mass flow rates (ratio ≈ ρair/ρwater ≈ 1.2/1000).
    • Manometer reading: trace from one end to the other. Go step by step: +ρgh going down, −ρgh going up, switching ρ at each fluid interface. Don't try to shortcut it.

    "Find the air/gas outflow" from a tank filling with liquidMass Conservation (RTT) with density ratio\(\dot{m}_{ ext{air}} = \dot{m}_{ ext{water}}
